subsubtopic: LICENSING OF SCALLOP FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my disappointment at the decision of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to withhold the renewal of licences for scallop fishermen for the 1987 season. During the Christmas break, in fact on December 29, 1986, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) released a press release indicating the plan for 1987. So much for openness by the Government which campaigned on that in the 1984 election. Once again an arbitrary decision was made by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans with no thought or consideration of the effect this measure will have on the lives and livelihoods of the fishermen affected.
In order to qualify for the new licences, fishermen must have landed scallops valued at $350 during any of the last five years. However, this arbitrary threshold ignores the fact that many fishermen simply do not sell their catch. Many keep the scallops for their own consumption, thereby significantly augmenting their over-all income, which is very limited. I call upon the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to rescind this order immediately and to end this unfair and arbitrary decision affecting the inshore fishermen of Nova Scotia and the Atlantic region.

Mr. Speaker, this being the week marking International Women's Day, all men and women must now ask themselves what progress has been accomplished since women took to the streets to claim their equality rights.
As women, Mr. Speaker, we are forced to conclude that even though there has been some progress at various Government levels since the Progressive Conservative Party took office, be it with respect to employment equity or appointments to the upper echelons of the Public Service, unfortunately some deplorable situations still remain in day-to-day life.
Specifically, violence against women in films, television and pornographic literature; minimum and hardly enforced sentences for sexual assaults against women; lack of adequate day care services; wage disparities, particularly in private industry; lack of social incentives with respect to sharing parental responsibilities, just to name a few.
Mr. Speaker, women did make some progress since they first demonstrated in public, but we have to admit that the fight is not over yet and that they still have a long way to go.

subsubtopic: U.S.S.R.-REUNIFICATION OF JEWISH FAMILIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise before the House today to comment on the plight of Soviet Jews. Many Jews have been denied the right of family reunification. Thousands of refusniks who have applied for exit have had their visas denied. More important, after a refusnik applies to leave, it seems that more often he or she is subject to being dismissed from his or her job. Furthermore, some have had their children expelled from school, some are being arbitrarily arrested, and some have had their personal property confiscated. Because of these Draconian measures, many more are afraid to apply for an exit visa to leave Russia.
When the Helsinki Accord was signed in 1975, one of the main principles agreed to was that participating states would deal in a positive humanitarian spirit with the applications of persons who wish to be reunited with members of their family. As a signatory to that accord, the Soviets have clearly not abided by this agreement.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to continue his good efforts in having the Soviets agree to allow these persecuted Jewish people the freedom to leave and join their loved ones in Israel and other nations around the world.

subsubtopic: ADVANTAGES OF HOUSING CO-OPERATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to a Co-operative Housing Foundation of Canada press release, a Gallup poll indicates widespread support for co-operative housing organizations: 72 per cent of respondents agree that housing co-operatives should be subsidized to give people an opportunity to find affordable
housing. There are a number of housing co-ops in Montreal, especially in my riding of Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic. Mr. Speaker, I was able to see for myself that this kind of housing offers advantages to the residents and the whole community.
In Canada last year, 3,500 new co-op units were built throughout the 10 provinces and two territories. Therefore the number of co-op housing units built in such remote localities as Yellowknife does not meet the demand.
I would urge the Minister responsible for housing to continue to make every effort to meet the needs of poorer Canadians. I would also urge him to find new solutions to provide more financial support to men and women who are not destitute enough to be eligible for Government assistance, yet not so well-off as to be able to find decent housing without having to tighten their belts unduly.

subsubtopic: IMPORTANCE OF SPECIAL MINING SHARES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's mining regions reacted very positively to the last Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Since February 19 I have been receiving calls to congratulate and thank us for maintaining the flow-through shares program. For many months I have been speaking out in support of this program, admirably seconded by the Quebec Prospectors Association and representatives from the mining industry in Abitibi-Temiscamingue and across this country.
Mr. Speaker, we made the point that the benefits of this financing program outweigh what it costs governments in loss of tax revenue. Flow-through shares are effective instruments for providing incentives to major economic activity in Canada's mining regions. Flow-through shares benefit the economically weaker northern regions of our provinces. Mr. Speaker, flow-through shares must be maintained under our upcoming tax reform.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF CO-OPERATIVE HOUSING PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a cross-Canada Gallup poll conducted in January of this year, 72 per cent of respondents agreed with the statement: "The Government should allocate subsidies for housing co-operatives as a way of providing affordable housing to Canadians". As well, 56 per cent of renters said they would be willing to try co-ops
March 4, 1987

themselves. Yet the Government went back on its promise to provide 5,000 co-op units per year. Instead, it is going ahead with only 3,200 units. This is a significant decline from previous years. It has as well reneged on its commitment to provide 1,500 rent supplemented co-op housing units for 1986. That number has been reduced to 950.
The Co-operative Housing Foundation, which is the voice of Canada's 1,100 non-profit housing co-operatives, wants to know why the federal Government is cutting back when Canadians are saying co-op housing is a high priority. Co-op housing has a proven record and strong public support. I call upon the Government to authorize the promised 5,000 co-op housing units and to release funds for the full 1,500 rent supplemented units.

subsubtopic: NUTRIENT VALUE OF BEEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate Canadian beef producers for meeting the needs of health conscious Canadians. Consumers can now be assured that the beef they serve their families is as low or lower in cholesterol than most other meats, including fish and chicken, while at the same time remaining a good source of iron and other essential nutrients.
I would also like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and Agriculture Canada for undertaking research to establish the latest figures on the healthfulness of Canadian beef. This data will now be included in the nutrient file of Health and Welfare Canada and its subsequent publication entitled "Nutrient Value of Some Common Foods". This is good news for all Canada.

subsubtopic: ANTI-BALLISTIC MISSILE TREATY-OPPOSITION TO REINTERPRETATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Paul Nitze, the senior adviser to the President on arms control, is coming to Ottawa this week to brief the Canadian Government on the White House's reinterpretation of the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty so as to enable extensive testing of the Strategic Defence Initiative known as star wars.
The response of the Canadian Government should be firm. There is no need for a reinterpretation of that treaty. Although it was signed only by the two superpowers, it is not a private contract to be nit-picked by lawyers in the Kremlin and the White House simply to provide new interpretations which
would permit the extensive testing of this new defensive system.
All humanity has a stake in that treaty. It is the very cornerstone of arms control. The reinterpretation which is sought by the United States could seriously jeopardize the future of arms control negotiations.

subsubtopic: SPOKESPERSONS' AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1983, the Liberal Party of Canada, today represented in the House by 40 Members with as many different positions, concluded an agreement with the United| States to allow the testing of Cruise missiles in Canada.
In November 1986 at their Party convention, those same Liberals decided to demand an end to the testing of U.S. Cruise missiles in Canada.
In February 1987, the official defence critic for the Liberal Party said that testing should be stopped immediately. Visibly embarrassed, the Leader of the party remarked that Liberal Members, even senior members, should not make statements on the missile issue on behalf of the Party. As soon as the Leader of the Liberal Party finished speaking, another member, the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri Westmount (Mr. Johnston), the Liberal critic for external affairs, said he agreed with his colleague from Sudbury.
The Liberal Leader was embarrassed again, and said rather awkwardly that he would have something to say when he had something to say.
Mr. Speaker, we knew that the Liberal Party of Canada had no ideas or programs or policies, but is it leaderless as well?

subsubtopic: SPECIAL CANADIAN GRAINS PROGRAM-CALCULATION OF PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are already some inequities showing in the Special Canadian Grains Program, the $1 billion assistance program to farmers. Some $700 million of the program remains to be paid out. The initial payment has been mailed out to farmers. It was based on a system of providing yield averages based on large crop insurance districts, as opposed to the average

March 4, 1987
Oral Questions
production potential of each farm, as was understood in the first place.
By using these large districts instead of actual farm production, inequities have crept in along the borders in particular. A 20 per cent or more difference exists between one road allowance and another where a farmer is caught in what is a relatively low-producing crop insurance district, even though his land is high-producing, comparable to the land of his neighbour across the road. This is creating inequities in the amounts of the payments.
As well, there are inequities in that producers of the so-called specialty crops are not covered even though their prices have fallen in response to the fall of the general market. Specialty crop prices reflect the market and are down by at least as much as the market for wheat, oats, and barley. The program should have covered those crops as well.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROMOTION CAMPAIGN BY DELEGATION VISITING EUROPE
ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROMOTION CAMPAIGN BY DELEGATION VISITING EUROPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a contingent of some 20 Canadian maritime and government officials is now taking part in a joint Canada-United States trade mission to northern Europe. The purpose of the mission is to promote greater use of the St. Lawrence Seaway-Great Lakes system. They have already met and were well-received by their counterparts in Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Finland. They have still to visit Dusseldorf, Antwerp and London.
The Canadian delegation is led by William O'Neil, President of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, along with representatives from two provinces, the users, and port and seaway officials. The delegation is joined by a 22-member contingent from the United States.
This mission, coupled with the federal Government's contribution of $175 million to rehabilitate the Welland Canal, is evidence of the Government's continuing support of the great Seaway system and its commitment to improving trade relations with northern Europe.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REOPENING OF STAR-KIST TUNA PLANT AT BAYSIDE, N.B.
speechtext:
Today, Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I met a delegation representing the former employees of the Star-Kist Canada Limited tuna packing plant in Bayside, New Brunswick.
The delegation's spokesman described for us the human tragedy which is afflicting this part of New Brunswick. Sixteen months have already elapsed since the closing of the plant which employed over 400 working men and women. The unemployment rate in this area currently reaches 36 per cent. These men and women want to work. They are recognized as the world's most productive fish processors.
Most of them have now run out of unemployment insurance benefits. Some have been placed in job creation projects, while others are on welfare.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote part of their presentation: "We beg of you today to give this matter the attention it deserves, to use all your powers to reopen the Bayside plant and make it possible for us to go back to work.''

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the Hon. Member's intervention. It should be very clear, if one examines the record, that the Government has always stood by Canadian farmers. subsubtopic: CARIBOU II-INQUIRY WHY WORK NOT STARTED IN QUEBEC SHIPYARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Last Monday, the Minister of Transport tried to pull a fast one on the people of British Columbia by telling employees at Versatile Pacific in Vancouver that their company would get the contract for the Polar 8 icebreaker, while in fact there was only a letter of intent from the Government to the company. Mr. Speaker, to Quebecers this story has a familiar ring, because the Conservative Government has announced three times over that work would start on the Caribou II, the ferry that was supposed to be built at the Versatile shipyards in Lauzon, and nothing has started yet. Could the Deputy Prime Minister explain to the House why, considering this contract was announced a year ago, in March 1986, work has yet to start at the Lauzon shipyards near Quebec City?

subsubtopic: CARIBOU II-INQUIRY WHY WORK NOT STARTED IN QUEBEC SHIPYARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member rose to his feet to get some elucidation on this issue. speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Privatization) and Minister responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next Sunday, March 8, will be International Women's Day. On that day, everywhere in Canada women will be taking an active part in the life of our society, as they do today and every day. At home, in their communities, and in every occupation and trade in our economy, women will be making an immeasurable contribution to our national wellbeing.
I am proud to sit in this House as the Minister responsible for the Status of Women.

Our Government takes its commitment to women very seriously. It means working nationally and internationally to advance the status of women. It means living up to our obligations under the United Nations Convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women and our commitment to implement the Nairobi Forward-Looking Strategies.
Since my appointment to this portfolio I have had the opportunity to meet many women in different regions of this country. Just a few weeks ago I travelled to Manitoba and met with and listened to a large number of women who are working with groups involved in worthwhile projects at the community level. This week I will be at Halifax and Wolfville, Nova Scotia, and then to Montreal to do more of the same.
These informal consultations have been an enriching experience. They provide me with a first-hand view of the situations women face in different parts of our country, and an appreciation of their goals, an appreciation of their lifestyles and their concerns. These first-hand experiences offer a perspective on Canada's changing demographics as influenced by the concerns of single mothers, the special needs of immigrant women, visible minority women, rural women, and urban women.
Meeting with them and their groups in their own region has enabled me to bring back to Ottawa the perspectives and perceptions of women from all across Canada. These conversations on every trip reinforce my commitment and dedication to, as well as my affection for the women of this land.

My mandate also includes chairing meetings and coordinating the Government's response to briefs submitted by women's groups on matters of principle. In recent months, my Cabinet colleagues and I met, with representatives of the Catholic Women's League, the National Council of Women of Canada and the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women.

March 4, 1987
Statements by Ministers
Through these meetings we keep abreast of positions taken by women's groups on various public interest issues, from child care to acid rain. The Government gives full consideration to their opinions and concerns when developing its policies and programs, in a concerted effort not to make decisions without first considering the repercussions they might have on the women of this country.
The concerns of women were high on the agenda of the March 1985 National Economic Summit. As a matter of fact, it was the first time such questions were one of the themes of a national economic conference. My colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) meets regularly with women's groups in the course of his pre-budget consultations. Last spring the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women set up a wide-ranging series of consultations with women's groups, and it has just concluded a national seminar on the family. I am pleased to point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and I had an opportunity to attend this seminar.
As Hon. Members know, the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women functions as a valuable channel to the Government for the concerns of women across the country. It is drawn from a variety of backgrounds, regions and perspectives and council members fill dual and crucial roles, both of advising the Government and of informing and educating the public on issues of concern to women. Over the years the Advisory Council has been in the forefront of identifying issues of importance to women and responding to these issues with policy recommendations and publications.
The Council's briefs and other presentations to the Government have dealt with such important issues as women's legal status under the Constitution, unemployment insurance, pornography, prostitution, child care, divorce and family maintenance and home-makers' pensions. In its recent publications, the Council has addressed such topics as wife battering, new directions in family law, adolescents' orientation to the future and women as health guardians in the home.
I am very pleased to see its new work plan for the next few years "Equal Status for Women in Canada in the 1990s". This is indeed a future oriented group.
Yesterday I had the pleasure of announcing a $.5 million permanent increase in the budget of the Council as recommended by the Government Task Force on Program Review. This increase will enable the Council to initiate relevant new research efforts and improve its ability to produce resource materials for new and expanded audiences. This expansion of the capabilities of the Advisory Council is further evidence of our Government's strong and unwavering commitment to the women of Canada. In the coming weeks and months, issues of interest to women will continue to be front and center on this Government's agenda.
Under the Prime Minister's leadership, our Government has brought women's concerns to the fore. Clear evidence of our commitment to women was provided in the document we published last fall Dimensions of Equality. A Federal Government Work Plan for Women. All Hon. Members of the House have received a copy. It is the first time a Government has produced a specific work plan on behalf of the women of Canada in order to give the country the knowledge and background to help us in our work on women's issues. Tabled by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) at the Annual Conference of First Ministers in Vancouver last November, there has been great demand for this book from across the land. It has turned out to be one of the best things we will continue to do.
Less than four months after its tabling, a number of work plan initiatives have already been accomplished or are well underway. For example, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) has announced that the Canadian Forces will conduct trials with women in combat roles. Also in keeping with the Government's commitment to expand the role of women in the Armed Forces, we have had the appointment of Canada's first woman General, Brigadier General Sheila Hellstrom, whom I am very proud to mention in the House today.
A review of sex stereotyping in internal Government communications is being completed. Labour Canada conducted an educational seminar for labour representatives on Equal Pay for Work of Equal Value. The Department of the Secretary of State funded a national conference held in Toronto as a follow-up to the 1985 Nairobi Forum and United Nations' World Conference on Women.

Discussions have begun with the provinces concerning child care. I will have more to say about this in a few minutes.
Last November there was a national conference of immigrant women and visible minority women, sponsored in part by the Secretary of State and Multiculturalism Canada.
The percentage of women appointed to various positions on Government boards, agencies and councils now stands at 27, so we are very close to the 30 per cent objective we had set for ourselves at the beginning.
These are only a few of the commitments towards women which our Government has honoured. Among some of our other achievements, I might mention the reform of legislation on divorce and alimony, and the repeal of the Indian Act provisions which for decades had been discriminatory towards native women.

As well, there is employment equity legislation, the establishment of a national training and employment program which, for the first time, sets participation targets for women, measures to expand and equalize pensions and the introduction of legislation to deal with the sexual abuse and exploitation of children.
March 4, 1987

At the First Ministers' Conference last November the Prime Minister described adequate child care as one of the most significant factors in ensuring the economic security of women. He has made a personal commitment to improve the accessibility, affordability, quality and flexibility of child care in Canada. I need not remind Hon. Members that child care is a serious national issue. It is a serious issue because first and foremost, it is about children, their future, their development and their place in our families and in our lives. It affects women, our society and our economy. Our Government is firmly convinced that an improved child care system will enable women who need or want to work to be in the labour force and to benefit from such a system. An improved system will provide opportunities for women to take the training programs. There is no point in having training programs if one cannot get out the door. There is no point in having employment equity if one cannot get out the door. On behalf of this Government, we want to give women the key which opens the door to opportunity and choice.
Public consultations have been a major focus for our Government thus far on the child care issue. We established a special Parliamentary Committee on Child Care with a mandate to seek information from a concerned public on this important debate. The committee conducted extensive crosscountry hearings and I am delighted to hear that the committee is expected to present its report to address these problems later this month.
[ Translation]
In the meantime, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has entered into consultations with the provinces which hopefully will lead to an agreement on improvements to the child care system by June 30. Clearly, that issue will remain at the forefront over the forthcoming months.
Women's health is another Government priority. It is obvious that women must be in good physical and mental health if they are to carry on with their numerous essential roles in our society. A good health care system is essential for women to realize their full potential.
The list of health issues of concern to women is a lengthy one. It includes access to health care, mental health, occupational and health safety, drug use and abuse, sexually-transmitted diseases and contraception. In particular, older women, disabled women, immigrant women and native women also have particular health concerns.
Our Government is responding to these concerns through the development of a health strategy for women. A vital component of the strategy will be a health promotion plan of action on aspects of women's lifestyles that are detrimental to their health. A number of research and demonstration projects on women's health issues are already being funded. Health and
Statements by Ministers
Welfare Canada is planning a symposium on the changing patterns of health and disease to take place in the spring of 1988.

A few weeks ago, I was made aware once again of the need for continuing research and awareness efforts on women's health needs when I visited the Women's Health Research Foundation in Winnipeg.
This volunteer, non-profit organization is promoting research on health matters that are closely connected with women. Last month, they sent to some thousand Manitobans a questionnaire aimed at establishing what problems and issues are considered by women to be important for their own health and welfare.
That kind of information is vitally needed to improve our health care system and get it to handle women's health needs with compassion and efficiency.
Our continuing consultations with women and women's groups have no other aim but to promote that exchange of information.

International Women's Day provides us with an opportunity to pay tribute to the achievements of the women of Canada. As Members of this House, we acknowledge that these are challenging times for women, and men, due to the changing demands of what is a transitional society. All Canadians are encouraged to realize their full potential. The Government is determined to ensure that in this process one's gender does not pre-determine the attainment of individual goals. International Women's Day gives us cause to reflect on these matters, to celebrate our progress and to prepare for the years ahead.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am also very happy to rise and address the House on behalf of Canadian women on International Women's Day.

This is a week in which women of all social status, all ages, single or married, mothers, single parents, housewives, students, workers and professionals can join in a common cause and celebrate the gains made for women over the years and their evolving role in Canadian society. It is also a week in which they can come together and inform the Government of urgent needs and demands that have yet to be satisfied. They can remind the present Government of all the promises made over the last two years and demand an accounting.
Canadian women are growing impatient with the endless rhetoric of the present Government. They are demanding a Government with the strength to act. The Minister said that the drop in the fertility rate could be the most important women's issue of the 1990s. I ask what the Government has done and is proposing to do about this issue. The fertility rate

March 4, 1987
Statements by Ministers
over the last 20 years has dropped from four births per woman in 1960 to 1.7 births per woman today. The birth rate in Canada is at a level at which it can just sustain the present population size and, by all accounts, the trend will continue downward and worsen.
We are in urgent need of research on fertility. Why are couples choosing to have fewer or no children? Can we do anything to reverse this trend? We need to know more about the ramifications of surrogate mothers and artificial insemination. The cost of raising children is prohibitive. It is possible that the presence of adequate and affordable child care is deterring people from having children. Yet the Government has been abysmally slow, postponing action on child care time and time again.
The Minister said that more and more women are entering the job market.
[ Translation]
As we know, two-thirds of Canadian women work outside the home, most of them are mothers, and 60 per cent of all women with children under three years old work outside the home. I would like to know what this Government is doing to help these women in the labour force.
As for Bill C-62 on Employment Equity, I was listening to the Minister praise this Bill, but I must admit that, in my opinion, it is toothless and is nothing but a collection of data in its present form.

The Government boasts about its Canadian Jobs Strategy Program, yet women complain that the majority of women participants are being trained for ghettoized jobs, clerical, service, sales and routine factory work, which pay low wages and are often seasonal or part-time. The federal Government has failed to fulfil its promises to provide prorated benefits to part-time workers. It has stalled again and again on child care. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) claims that his commitment to child care is real. Women cannot achieve equality in the workplace without child care. Women are tired of empty promises. They want affordable, accessible child care services now, not five years down the road.
The recent Budget did not set aside one penny for child care. How can the Government keep pledging its commitment to this issue in good conscience?
[ Translation]
The Minister indicated recently that four out of 10 marriages ended in divorce and that the majority of singleparent families have a woman as head of the household and live under the poverty line. I would like to know what the Government is doing for these families.
If we refer to the budget brought down in late February, we find that families with an income of $15,000 or less were hit with a 53 per cent tax increase, while families with an income of $100,000 and more have seen their taxes increase by 6 per cent over the last three years.
The Government has also made plans and promises to create a central agency to deal with divorce cases. In my opinion, the Divorce Act still does not reflect the promises made by the Federal Government to Canadian women. It is still impossible to find, or rather, the defaulting husband can perhaps be found, but all that the Government does is to provide an address and say to which province the husband has moved, but a woman who wants to receive her support payments must initiate proceedings in another province and often wait up to three years before getting any money. I therefore do not think that the Government has made that much progress in the area of divorce and kept its promise to Canadian women.
Naturally, there is nothing about the promises regarding part-time work. The Government has done absolutely nothing about part-time work and pension benefits for homekeepers. There is no mention either of housing, even though the neediest families are those without proper housing and the Government has made drastic cutbacks in its housing program.
The Minister knows that one out of 10 Canadian women is a victim of family violence. Again, what is the Government doing about this problem? Last year the budget of the Family Violence Information Centre was cut. The Government underfunds transitional houses for battered women. This action implies that women's issues are not the priority that the present Government pretends. Action in dollars makes programs, not rhetoric.
The Prime Minister said that for many women child care is the key to future equality. Only 9 per cent of the children in need of day care receive approved services. Approximately 60 per cent of Canadian mothers are in the workforce, and many are in desperate need of affordable, accessible, flexible, quality child care. So far we have had nothing but words on this issue, pages and pages of suggestions, but not one penny toward a viable national child care system.

A recent poll indicated that two-thirds of Canadians support a universal day-care system. I would really like to know when the Government will do something about this.

Is this simply a publicity campaign? Is the Government stalling so that it can present a comfortable package before the next election?
The Conservative Government was eager to attract women, 52 per cent of the Canadian electorate, and it made all manner of promises. To date there has been the deindexation of family allowance, an increase in federal sales and excise tax which hurts lower and middle income families, cut-backs on programs for training women, cut-backs on transition houses for battered women, and nothing but words and vague promises on the child care issue. The three big Conservative promises that would involve government expenditure and action, namely,
March 4, 1987

home-maker pensions, pro-rated benefits for part-time workers, and the national child care system, have turned out to be empty promises.
I mentioned before that it gave me great pleasure to address the House on this subject during International Women's Week. Having said that, I urge the Government to follow up on these many promises and show a true commitment to women across Canada and their concerns.

There have been many promises, discussions and consultations, but little action. In my opinion, consultations carried out without listening, responding and acting are not of much use to Canadian women.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I owe an apology to my friends, the Hon. Member for Out-remont (Mrs. Pepin), and the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). I made a reference to their not asking questions earlier this week. I understand that after agreement with my office it was decided that we would wait until the statements were made before we asked questions together in the House. Like many things, it totally escaped my notice, for which I apologize.

Mr. Speaker, since 1910 women around the world have met on March 8 to celebrate International Women's Day. We meet to celebrate the achievements of women, to share our knowledge and experience, to extend mutual support networks, and to reenergize so that we can continue to press for changes that are needed on the long road to equality.
Canadian women hold out their hands in solidarity to women in other countries as we work in our own ways for the forward-looking strategies endorsed in Nairobi in 1985. Canadian women provided outstanding leadership at that conference. Our Governments have been slower in implementing these strategies here at home.
We stand in solidarity with women around the world who are working for peace and an end to nuclear arms, in order that the world's children can grow in safety and in health. We ask our Government to work more aggressively for disarmament, and to show its commitment by immediately cancelling the new five-year agreement to test nuclear Cruise missiles.
We stand in solidarity with African women, and women in other Third World countries who are struggling for survival, and who bear impossible burdens, particularly those who bear the burden of apartheid. We ask our Government to implement full economic sanctions against South Africa. We also ask for increased funding for CIDA programs for women in development.
We stand in solidarity with women of Latin American whose loved ones have disappeared, who suffer from the violence of war and dictatorships and oppressive patriarchal relationships. We ask our Government to be more sensitive to
Statements by Ministers
these women and their families, and to welcome those who seek refuge in Canada.
We also ask our Government to provide more support, including language and job training with child care for immigrant women. We urge measures to counteract the racism that visible minority women experience in Canada.
Native women who apply for reinstatement to Indian status face many difficulties. We ask the Government to provide the additional resources that were promised to Indian communities to accommodate resettlement.
Canadian women fought for and won equality under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This was a great legal achievement. But we have not yet achieved equality in fact. Rather than patting itself on the back, we ask the Government to listen to what Canadian women are saying. Many fear that we may be going backward from equality objectives. Unfortunately, I have to say that this movement is being led by some elected Members of the House.
On behalf of many Canadian women, I ask the Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mrs. McDougall) to be a stronger advocate and conscience within the Government for women's rights. We ask her to be outspoken and active in removing obstacles that women face, rather than defending government positions. In particular, I ask that the Minister reconsider and reform employment equity to make it mandatory in order that women have equal job opportunities with equal pay for work of equal value in all federally-related jobs. This would be a great initiative, and a model for other employers to emulate.
I ask the Minister to review the Canadian Jobs Strategy program, and to work with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to remove the barriers and improve both training and job opportunities for women. We also ask her to meet with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) to implement changes in the Canada Labour Code to cover prorated wages and benefits for part-time workers.
We also ask the Minister, as a women's advocate, to analyse the impacts on women of free trade, deregulation, and privatization policies of the Government. Women are worried that once again they will be the last hired and the first fired.
Feminization of poverty has escalated, particularly for women who are raising children alone. We ask that the Government exempt low income people from taxes, and call for an increase in family benefits with reindexation of family allowances. We urge tax reforms that will redistribute incomes more fairly, along with a concerted attack on poverty through a full employment program and income security policies.
The Minister has said that the Government takes its commitment to women seriously. These are serious concerns of Canadian women which the Government must address. Yesterday the Minister allocated $500,000 to the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, for which I congratulated her. Will the Minister also advocate increases to

March 4, 1987
Committee Reports
Secretary of State women's programs which were cut back in funds by 5 per cent last year? This means that women's groups in the front line out there in communities are very short of funds, and many centres are closing down. Will she reaffirm that the objective of equality must be the basis for future funding under this Secretary of State program so that we can continue to improve equality for women? We commend the Government for increasing the appointments of women to various positions and as Deputy Ministers. If only we could adopt a policy of gender parity in the House of Commons, how changed this place might be.
Finally, the Minister talked about child care and women's health programs. Need I say once again that the Government's goodwill toward child care will only be evident when it allocates federal bucks for Canada's children. Federal initiatives and leadership are essential as a precedent to negotiating shared funding for child care with the provinces. Will the Minister not ask that the $300 million, which we discovered in reserve funds in the social development envelope in the current Estimates, be named for federal child care initiatives as an act of good faith?
Questions affecting women's health and well-being have been neglected for too long in Canada. A top priority should be a program of research into safe and effective methods of contraception for both men and women. A secondary area is the need to study carefully, with the full participation of women, new reproductive technologies to develop a sound and ethical policy in Canada.
I know I have not covered many issues, including increasing violence, pornography, and sexual abuse. Women stand together and demand that this abuse must stop. On behalf of the New Democratic Party, I extend warm greetings, in sisterhood and in solidarity, to Canadian women on Sunday, March 8, in celebration of International Women's Day.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLLUTION-EMISSION REDUCTION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
That this House deplores the government's failure to pursue effectively federal-provincial agreements with the result that the Conservative Governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia remain reluctant to sign S02 emission reduction agreements, thus jeopardizing the credibility of the Canadian acid rain program;
That this House also deplores the fact that, two years after the Quebec summit meeting, no benefits to Canada in the form of S02 emission reductions in the United States have materialized; and
That, therefore, this House urges the government to:
(1)	pursue vigorously the implementation of agreements on S02 emission
reductions with the Provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and
(2)	request at the April, 1987 summit meeting that the United States reduce
S02 emissions over the Canadian border in a significant manner.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in putting this motion before the House today, we in the Opposition do so because we feel that this issue is of public concern right across the country; a matter about which Canadians are deeply and understandably exercised, and in doing so we are making a contribution to the understanding of this issue as it stands presently. We are advancing ideas in the hope that we will eventually arrive at the desired goal of cutting emissions that effect acid rain to the point where the environment around us, human health and other factors will benefit.
The motion itself is couched in the words that express regrets about the situation in which we find ourselves both domestically and internationally, but they are expressed in the form of regret rather than accusations or sharp criticism, because we know that in essence this is an issue that unites all Canadians. It brings together all three Parties in this House. It brings together federal and provincial Governments to a considerable degree at least, and it is an issue about which
Canada has become known abroad as a strong engine in the search for solutions. We want to approach this matter today in a constructive manner, keeping in mind of course that the design of this House and the parliamentary system to which we belong do encourage constructive criticism. It was in that spirit that the motion today was drafted.
I would like to confirm to you, Mr. Speaker that we on this side of the House in my Party applauded the Government in 1984 when it took such an interest in the question of acid rain. We saw it as a desirable continuation in pursuing public interest in a manner that transcended political viewpoints and, in a way rightly or wrongly, as a continuation of the work that had been initiated in preceding years on which I will dwell in a moment or two. It has become quite evident though that we disagree on the process. How do we get there? We certainly agree on the substance of what we want to achieve. We disagree, for instance, on how we should convince the Americans to come on board. We feel that we should not pursue the route of research and demonstration projects, but we know that that is one way of keeping the theme alive.
When it was announced, as a result of the summit a year or so ago, that that was the route which the federal Government intended to take on behalf of all of us, we thought we should give it a chance, because maybe it is the way to proceed. But if we look at the continuum of this process, we find some very important dates in the history and in the saga of acid rain. We find, of course, the agreement of February, 1985 which was a federal-provincial agreement. It was preceded by the agreements that took place in March and June, 1984 between the federal and the provincial Governments, which were also preceded by the conclusion that very same year that we had to go it alone if the Americans did not want to proceed. All of these were preceded in 1980 by the memorandum of intent, to which I understand you, Mr. Speaker, also had a role to play, that we must see this thing over a period of several years as a continuum and as an evolution of policy in the public interest.
At this stage, March 4, we have to express profound regret that no provinces, two years and one month after another confirmation of the agreement of February, 1985 on acid rain, have yet signed and that two provinces, namely, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, seem to have profound problems in adhering and sticking to the understanding and to the agreement itself. In that respect, we are fully supportive of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and of the Government of Canada, that that agreement has got to stick and has to be respected by the provinces, which was understood clearly by all the participants at the meeting of February, 1985, as it was fully understood in June 1984 and in March 1984.
There was a division of labour. The responsibility of reducing acid rain emissions was divided in two parts. It was said, "You, the provinces, take the responsibility of cutting down your emissions through your utilities, because utilities are provincial, and the federal Government will take on the economic burden of modernizing the smelters". It was
March 4, 1987

envisaged that this responsibility would require substantial funds as well, but, nevertheless, something that could be done by way of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of Industry at the time and, therefore, it was a reasonable division of labour. The provinces present, through their Ministers of the Environment at the time understood very well this division of labour.
At this stage we find it impossible to understand why the Province of New Brunswick and the Province of Nova Scotia would, all of a sudden develop, double talk on this issue, would waiver and indicate that they cannot deliver on a commitment that is just two years and one month old.
The agreement also includes certain important considerations. The Government of Canada in February, 1985 did say that it would make available $150 million for smelter modernization-fine. It also said that for the development of a clean coal technology, which is the important message to the provinces, that it would make available $70 million. Yesterday during questioning in the special committee on acid rain we learned to our amazement that of the $70 million, $35 million has been used by the Province of New Brunswick, by the New Brunswick Power Commission, without any recognition that this amount somehow came from Ottawa and without any indication that that was something the province would appreciate in order to resolve the problem. Half of the amount has been used and so far we have not seen any political expression or will to come on board.
There is also an amount of $25 million for technology development announced as part of the package, as well as research and monitoring funds to an extent of $18 million per year. You can see that the totality of the package is there. The division of labour was announced and explained. The political representatives of the provinces, as mature adult responsible individuals, said yes. Some are coming through. We were told in committee that several provinces are doing what they agreed to, and some are even doing more, as in the case of Ontario. The Province of Manitoba is sticking to its commitment and the Province of Quebec is doing its part too. For the life of us, the members of the committee, we cannot understand why the two provinces, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, are not carrying their share, which is actually one of the lowest burdens requested to be carried of all the provinces.
The fact that there is to be an upcoming summit is another reason we are debating this matter today. It is another link in the long chain I mentioned a moment ago, beginning with the Memorandum of Intent of August 1980. I will not bother you, Mr. Speaker, with all the developments that have taken place since, but it seems to us that on the eve of this important meeting between the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mul-roney) and the President of the United States, a good debate in the House is not only appropriate but is absolutely essential. I look forward to hearing the Minister's and my colleagues' analyses of today's situation.
Supply
It is urgent, therefore, that both New Brunswick and Nova Scotia sign the federal-provincial agreements at the earliest possible date with an indication before the summit as to when they will do so. They have been given two years to carry out that assignment. I suppose the Minister, through his officials, has pursued the matter frequently. I suppose there is a group of officials constantly negotiating the matter so as to bring it to a conclusion. Surely the Prime Minister will not want to go to the summit in April without having closed ranks behind him, without having all the provinces saying that they are ready to deliver and do their share.
The whole policy was based on the premise that we must go to the Americans with clean hands. I must confess that I had some reservations about that approach because there is such a difference between the forces. We emit 4.5 million tonnes a year while the U.S. emits somewhere between 24 million and 25 million tonnes of S02 per year. Even if we go to them with clean hands we will still face damage to the environment, lakes, forests, the aquatic systems, structures and human health. There will be an amount of S02 that will still be threatening us because we are downwind of it. Even if we come through perfectly clean, we will still be damaged. Nevertheless, it was a good gesture.
You will forgive me, Mr. Speaker, if I lack that sense of modesty for which you know me so well when I say that it was actually in February 1984 when Ruckelshaus came back from negotiations with the White House empty handed that we said that we must go it alone because there was no alternative. We said that we could not wait forever in the hope that somehow something would be triggered. We made that decision, and I am sure the present Minister has renewed it himself on a number of occasions, knowing very well that it needed an enormous degree of political commitment because of our uncertainty as to whether or not the Americans would follow. I suppose it was in that light that the decision to go the Lewis-Davis route of further research was made. Having gone that far, the reluctant provinces must come on board.
There is another main thrust of today's motion. We should take the cue of the present Minister of the Environment. On January 22, 1987 he said that U.S. clean coal initiatives will be of no immediate help to Canada. I felt that it took courage to say that. I congratulated him. I suppose he said what he did because his own officials delivered to him a study he had requested last November. He was giving a signal, not only to us in the Opposition, because we watch these things like hawks, but to his own Government as well. He was saying that the approach of further research and demonstration projects was not working. Yes, we agree fully that the U.S. coal initiative is of no immediate help to Canada. Therefore, the second part of our motion urges the Government of Canada to be clear in communicating its message to the U.S. and to say clearly that it wants a significant reduction in S02 emissions that are transboundary and affect our economy, our environment and our health. That is what we really want.

March 4, 1987
Supply
There must come a point when we must make a decision as to how to invest our time. It is our perception of the matter at least, and I am sure it is the perception of the Minister in his own private moments when he turns off the light at night to go to bed, that we must ask ourselves if we have not reached the point at which we must stress a new tack. We must ask ourselves if we should not say openly and frankly, as one must among friends, that the quality of our relations with the U.S. will be affected and will deteriorate more and more the longer the White House ignores the message calling on it to take action of substance, not further research.
We were very heartened when we read a statement made by U.S. Senator Mitchell the other day. On January 16, in presenting his Bill, he concluded that he would also continue to press the administration to change its view that everything must be known before anything can be done. He is saying that we cannot have 100 per cent scientific assurances but that there is a point when we must act. We cannot wait for the last "i" to be dotted and the last "t" to be crossed. He said that each year we wait the cost of not taking action increases and that the price already paid is already too high. We are fully behind that statement and we know that there is a North-South alliance on the matter of acid rain. We in Canada are not alone. Congressmen and Senators are saying the same things as we are saying.
The time has probably come to renew our lobby in Washington and to renew the efforts of those who are on the side of the Staffords and Mitchells of this world. Whichever Government will be in power when we succeed, bully for it; we will applaud it from this side of the House because we all feel the same way. We are telling the Minister to tell it like it is, to ask for emission cuts and to push the provinces. We are telling him that we are 100 per cent behind him when he asks the provinces to stick to their commitment. They made that commitment in the full knowledge of what it meant and they must deliver. We will do our duty along with the Hon. Member from Muskoka by pressing the matter in committee. We might have taken a different tack. It would have been very tempting to ask embarrassing questions, but we refrained from doing so. We can assure the Minister and the Government that on this matter we have the same determination as he, but we are asking him to change at last Canada's position at the next summit because it is time to say it like it is. We want emission cuts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLLUTION-EMISSION REDUCTION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for that diversion. Some points of order bear repetition when the opportunity presents itself.
We welcome the motion moved today by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). It gives us the opportunity to debate the whole question of acid rain. This issue is high on the Canadian political agenda and has been for some time, but it is particularly important this week and in the coming weeks as we near the summit meeting between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States, where we expect acid rain to be discussed, and hope against hope that action will be forthcoming as a result of that meeting.
The motion states:
That this House deplores the government's failure to pursue effectively federal-provincial agreements with the result that the Conservative Governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia remain reluctant to sign S02 emission reduction agreements, thus jeopardizing the credibility of the Canadian acid rain program;
Anyone who is concerned about this issue knows that I am not an apologist for the Government, but the failure in this narrow respect lies with the Conservative Governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and not necessarily with the

March 4, 1987
Supply
federal Conservative Government. Those two provincial Governments have failed to take seriously their agreements with the federal Government in 1985 that they would arrive at subsequent detailed agreements with the federal Government to reduce acid rain emissions in their own provinces. I suggest that nothing has changed to warrant the Governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia pulling out of this agreement at the last minute. They are doing so at a very inopportune moment, when the Prime Minister ought to be able to show evidence of as much progress as possible when meeting with President Reagan in April.
Yet two provincial Conservative Governments are moving at the last minute to undermine the Prime Minister, and I expect that when the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) speaks today he will explain how the Government will address this action by those two provincial Governments.
The Special Committee on Acid Rain is considering calling the Premier of New Brunswick before the committee to hear why the Government of New Brunswick has acted in this way. We have already heard from the New Brunswick Power Corporation. I must say that the reasons it gave why it was unable to live up to the agreement were insufficient. Not only is it jeopardizing the credibility of the Canadian Government in this respect, it is jeopardizing the credibility of Canada's collective political determination to do something about acid rain. In the final analysis, that is more important than the credibility of the Government.
The Government does have a credibility problem insofar as it has backed down on the deadlines for the institution of nitric oxide emission controls and has not instituted as quickly as possible emission controls on heavy vehicles, and this reflects badly on Canada, but the lack of action on the part of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia is not the Government's fault.
Let me turn to Manitoba which I believe is proceeding toward an agreement. The Manitoba Government faces a much more difficult question because it is dealing with the modernization of a very old smelter in the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting operation in Flin Flon. The situation is much more delicate than that facing New Brunswick Power and Nova Scotia Power who do not have to worry about a disappearing market. The people of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia will continue to require electricity. Unlike Manitoba, New Brunswick Power and Nova Scotia do not face the prospect of shutting down if the acid rain negotiations are unsuccessful or if proper funding and restructuring is not provided. However, there is a political will in Manitoba to do something about acid rain, and progress is being made in spite of these difficulties.
The Governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia cannot be excused for pulling out of this agreement at the last minute, thereby putting the Prime Minister and Canada in a very difficult situation and, most significant, damaging our credibility on this issue.
We have heard the argument about coming to the table with clean hands. That is not the most important argument and the Hon. Member for Davenport made a good point when he said that such a strategy has its limits. In the final analysis, we must deal with the sheer magnitude of the damage being done to the Canadian environment by American emissions. That is the environmental fact which must override these petty arguments about who will do what and when.
The Canadian environment is at stake, and this, in turn affects the very essence of Canada-U.S. relations. Let me give this analogy. How long would one continue calling a neighbour a friend when that neighbour consistently pollutes one's backyard and garden, and makes the neighbourhood playground uninhabitable for children? How long would one continue to call that person a neighbour, let alone a friend?
The Special Committee on Acid Rain met with a number of American journalists earlier today. The point I made at our meeting with them was the same, that it is not only an environmental question, but a fundamental question of Canada-U.S. relations.
With respect to the process, the motion goes on to state:
That this House also deplores the fact that, two years after the Quebec summit meeting, no benefits to Canada in the form of S02 emission reductions in the United States have materialized;
Unfortunately, this is not a great surprise to a great many people. There was a lot of feeling at the beginning of the very first summit that the approach being taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was not going to work, that he had far too high an expectation of what could be produced as a result of the new relationship he sought to enter into with the President of the United States.
I think the Prime Minister set himself up rather badly by creating expectations that anyone who was paying any attention knew were unrealistic expectations. It was a process, one might say in retrospect, that was destined for failure partly because of the hyperbole of the Prime Minister and that of the Government still today with respect to what it has accomplished. We still hear members on the government side talking about what they have accomplished, that for the first time the Americans have realized that acid rain is a problem. We heard that even today. It is not the first time that Americans have realized that acid rain is a problem either at the administrative level or the congressional level. It is the first time the Reagan administration acknowledged there was a problem, yes. Within the context of the Reagan administration, that is progress. When there is someone who, as the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is fond of saying, thinks that acid rain might come from ducks, who then admits it actually comes from emissions from industry, I suppose that is progress. However, it is not something I would get up and dance about. It is not something on which I would hinge the credibility of my approach to Canada-U.S. relations. Yet that appears to be
March 4, 1987

the only thing the Government can point to or, at least, that is what it persistently does point to.
In the final analysis, what needs to be impressed upon all Governments and everyone concerned with this issue is the inevitable and unavoidable economic costs of not doing anything about acid rain. We have to be able to do our bookkeeping in a fundamentally different way than that fragmented, piecemeal way whereby everyone takes into account how their own books look, whether it is Inco, the Province of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick Power or the West Virginia Coal Company, whoever it happens to be. We must find a way of doing the kind of global ecological bookkeeping which enables us to make over-all political decisions about what is in the best interests of the environment and, therefore, in the best interests of the economy. We cannot build a healthy, sustainable and just economic future on the basis of an environment which is slowly but surely being eaten away every day by acid rain.
I do not know if Hon. Members have heard this story, but the nature of environmental destruction is such that it progresses geometrically rather than arithmetically. That is to say that we never know at what point the damage may quadruple, or whatever, in such a way that we are faced with a very different situation from that which we were able to predict only a short time ago. I think we are in that position with respect to forestry, for instance. Five years ago not even West Germany, where it is most advanced, was aware that there was anything like the significant reduction in tree growth. Yet in Canada, it is now established that there is a two-thirds reduction in growth in trees. I ask Hon. Members to imagine, for the sake of trying to understand how these problems develop, a pond which will be progressively covered by lily pads. It starts out with one lily pad and it will take 28 days for that vegetation to cover the pond. At first there is one lily pad and then there are two lily pads, then four, then eight, then 16, then 32, then 64, then 128. The fact is that if it takes 28 days to cover this pond with lily pads, on the twenty-seventh day half the pond will still be left, but we only have one day to go. With many of these environmental questions, we do not know whether we are in the twenty-fifth day, the twenty-sixth day or the twenty-seventh day, and there are people in industry, in politics and elsewhere, both in Canada and the United States, who say: "Do not worry about it. We have half the pond left. What are all you environmentalists worried about?". The way in which environmental problems progress is as I have just described it. I ask people to think about that because that is our situation with respect to acid rain.
I do not know at what day we are now. I do not believe anyone does. However, I do know there are not that many days left before we will have done irreversible damage to our environment.
I spoke earlier about the economic costs, and a good example of that is what is happening in Quebec.
Supply

With respect to the impact of acid rains in Quebec, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give as an example the serious situation in that province, particularly concerning the future of sugar bushes. As a result of acid rains, the degradation of forests, and maple groves in particular, is progressing rapidly over the whole Quebec territory. According to the Quebec Agricultural Producers Union, Quebec maple syrup producers have already lost at least two million taps because of acid rains, and such losses are increasing at an alarming rate. APU spokesmen also estimate that the loss is already worth $87 million and, should degradation continue, it will threaten the livelihood of 10,000 Quebec maple syrup producers. Worse still, these figures do not take into account the acid rain impact on the other forest industries, nor on tourism or fisheries.
Mr. Speaker, air pollutants, especially acid rain, are the cause of major social and environmental losses in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada. This Government should take decisive action. First and foremost, this Government, and especially the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), should adopt a more aggressive attitude toward the Reagan administration. Faced with an ecological and economic disaster it is time, for the Prime Minister to explain to Mr. Reagan the bitter resentment felt by all Canadians toward the American's lack of action in the fight against acid rain, and to emphasize the need for the Americans to take concrete action to reduce air pollution affecting Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I have always had a great deal of respect for the interventions of the Hon. The fact of the matter is that part of the problem with the debate has been the caricaturing of the two approaches taken by the Liberal Government prior to 1984 and the Conservative Government after 1984. It is not the case that the Liberal Government was kicking, screaming, yelling and throwing verbal hand-grenades at Washington. It is not the case that the current Government has done nothing but be obsequious, create false expectations or be totally gullible. There are elements of truth in both those caricatures. But, in the final analysis, they are caricatures.
What we have not considered when we debate what approach will be most successful is whether or not we can be successful. We have not considered whether or not there is not some point at which the Canadian people would appreciate the honest admission of failure and acknowledgement that there may be some things that neither approach will accomplish. Maybe it is in the nature of the United States of America that whether one kicks the Americans in the shins or whether one slaps them on the back they will not do anything that is not in their self-interest. Perhaps that is the conclusion we have to draw first before we can begin to have a real debate about the matter, as opposed to the phoney debate to which the Hon. Member just contributed with respect to whether or not the approach of the present Government or the last Government will work. All of this is based on the assumption that there is some sort of magical button that neither Government has yet found and pushed that will bring the United States into line on these types of issues.
I am sorry to say that the history of the United States is not that there are magical buttons which one can push, either rhetorically, at summits, or on stages singing When Irish Eyes Are Smiling. Nor is there any other measure that might have been taken by the previous Liberal Government. Perhaps what we need to do is to get down to business instead of playing the game that if somebody would only do what the other guy advises them to do we would be so much more successful.
And if the Prime Minister does not come up with some significant advance with respect to acid rain at the summit it is my best political advice to him that he come out and say so. He should say that he did his best for the people of Canada but that he is up against a nation which is known for its selfcentredness and for the fact that it is one of the most powerful nations in the world. speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLLUTION-EMISSION REDUCTION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by saying to the mover of the motion that I genuinely welcome the motion itself, while expressing some regret about its negative tone. Given the fact that the Hon. Member has an obvious commitment to the issue, and given his efforts as a Minister of the Crown in the previous Government to make progress on it, I am sure that he would be the last to want to leave any impression that his Party is playing politics with an issue that has traditionally transcended partisanship.
I remind the Hon. Member and the House of the two landmark reports of the parliamentary Subcommittee on Acid Rain, the one to which I was a contributor entitled Still Waters, and the later document, Time Lost. They received the unanimous support of all Parties in the House.
This motion today could not come at a more delicate time. The Government is at a crucial point in negotiations with the seven eastern provinces from Manitoba to Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, and with the United States. In the
Supply
case of the provinces, the Government is in the throes of negotiating individual agreements to implement the commitments they made as separate provinces, and collectively, in February, 1985. With the United States we are working to achieve not only full implementation of the celebrated Special Envoy's recommendations, but also action to substantially reduce the transboundary flow of pollution into Canada from the United States.
Notwithstanding the critical flavour of the motion, and the fact that Members of the House may differ on details as to how to cope with acid rain-causing emissions, I think it can be said there are no differences among us on the over-all objective. There can be no doubt about the supreme importance that the federal Government attaches to finding long-term lasting solutions to acid raid. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has made acid rain not only his number one environmental priority, but also his primary agenda item with the United States among the myriad of bilateral issues with which we as a Government are wrestling. The Prime Minister is the first Canadian head of Government to make acid rain a personal, individual priority. In doing so he has elevated the profile of the issue at home and abroad, including the United States, where public awareness has soared in recent months. I must say that I am a little discouraged that the Prime Minister has not been given more credit, or more encouragement, within the House and the country at large for at least trying.
The mover of the motion may recall a different situation before the Government took office. I do not draw the attention of the House to this point in order to paint caricatures of us as good guys over here, and them the bad guys over there. I am putting today's debate in an historical context. In August, 1980, the Minister of the Environment prior to the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), for whom I had great respect, signed a Memorandum of Intent with the United States. He had the good grace to do it when I was in Lahaina. For all the high hopes at that time little real progress was made on the Memorandum of Intent signed in August, 1980. I am not critical of the Government for its lack of progress with the United States, because the conditions that then made progress difficult continue to prevail now, making it difficult for this Government to move the American elephant even one step on the issue. In June, 1982, only months after the Memorandum of Intent was signed, committing the two Governments to solid action on acid rain, the previous Government broke off formal negotiations with the United States out of sheer frustration. No progress can be made on any issue by any Government when the principals are not present at the negotiating table.
The now Prime Minister assessed the situation while Opposition Leader. He arrived at two conclusions as Prime Minister prior to the March 1985 Shamrock Summit in Quebec with the President of the United States. The Prime Minister stated that if Canada is to make any progress with the United States, it must have the moral authority based on a "clean-hands" approach to acid rain within our own borders.

March 4, 1987
