Literally speaking, we had to put our money where our commitment was. Second, the Prime Minister stated that we needed a process that would bring the United States back to the bargaining table. The process had to recognize existing positions, especially the one taken by the United States at that time namely, that acid rain is not a problem, let alone something that should be elevated to the top of the agenda of the two countries. Needed too was a mechanism for moving the issue forward. With no small amount of effort in the space of two and a half years, the Prime Minister, the Government, and the country, because it is a non-partisan issue, have achieved some real progress on those two objectives.
I wish to deal with what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), and indeed the Prime Minister, has called our "clean hands" policy. Almost six months after the new Government took office in February, 1985, my predecessor reached what I think we can all agree was an important accord with our colleagues from the seven eastern provinces from Manitoba through to Newfoundland. The eight Governments, including the federal Government itself, agreed to reduce total Canadian sulphur dioxide emissions in Canada to 2.3 million tonnes, which was a 50 per cent reduction based on 1980 figures. Each province agreed to a specific reduction program within its borders as a contribution to the total national emission reduction effort. They agreed to enforce their respective programs through legislation or other fiats, and to do so by 1994 at the latest.
The provincial emission limits were not developed by the federal Government and imposed by it on the participating provinces. The control program was not shoved down their throats. The provincial limits were volunteered by individual provinces as their contribution to a great national cause. I stress the fact that commitments were made by each province as much to one another as to the federal Government.
It was not an agreement between the seven provinces on the one hand and the federal Government on the other. It was an agreement among eight Governments to one another and to the people of Canada. The federal Government was acting as the glue holding together a compact among different Governments and different jurisdictions.
The federal role in the February 1985 accord was clear. We agreed that if financial assistance was deemed necessary for the actions required at non-ferrous smelters, we would take the lead as the federal Government in arranging it.
Why was this commitment limited to smelters? I think that is an important question in the context of the motion we are debating today, especially vis-a-vis Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It was for two good reasons. First, smelters are responsible for most of the sulphur dioxide emissions in eastern Canada. Second, the provinces clearly indicated themselves that they wanted the lead in dealing with their own utilities. The coal question, the thermal power coal question, revolves
around provincial utilities in Nova Scotia, in New Brunswick, and in Ontario, for that matter.
In any event, why should federal tax dollars be used to subsidize profitable provincial utilities, no matter how noble the cause might be? That question was asked by the provinces themselves when the agreement was reached in February, 1985. As the federal Government's part of the bargain, Cabinet agreed to provide up to $150 million to share the costs of smelter modernization-pollution abatement initiatives required to achieve provincial emission limits, as well as a further $150 million for research and development and demonstration projects.
All eight parties to the February 1985 accord knew exactly what they were doing at the time. There was no hidden agenda, no fact concealed, no possible eventuality raised, and no condition attached to the agreement. It would be reprehensible now, 24 months later, for any party or any Government, provincial or federal, to renege on its commitment. There can be no ransom, no changing of terms, no procrastination based upon limp-wristed concerns about what might happen in future if this or that were to happen and specific control measures were thereby made more difficult to achieve.
The eight Governments must all stay the course. If some unforeseen circumstance should make it difficult for one or other of the partners to do so between now and 1994, I am sure the others will want to help it so as to keep the pact intact.
What sense does it make now, in the late winter of 1987, to be worrying about some possible circumstance in 1992 or 1994 which would cause us to rethink what we agreed to in February 1985? For my part, I intend to begin soon signing on behalf of this jurisdiction the formal federal-provincial acid rain abatement agreements necessary to ratify the original February 1985 compact among the different Governments.
Cabinet has authorized allocation of funds for the smelter modernization-pollution abatement program. The cash is there. It has been set aside. It has been committed. Manitoba will have up to $20 million; Ontario, up to $85 million; and Quebec, up to something like $42 million.
Some observers claim that the Atlantic provinces are being denied assistance for the acid rain clean-up. They see the millions of dollars for Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec and no money for New Brunswick or Nova Scotia, and ask; Aren't we as federal and provincial Governments discriminating against eastern Canada?
I am an Atlantic Canadian. I come from Prince Edward Island. My mother was a British Columbian. I derive no pleasure, no pride, and no satisfaction from the fact that at the eleventh hour we are making some efforts to unravel the ball of yarn.
The truth is that there is no discrimination. Under the Energy, Mines and Resources coal utilization program, about $70 million in federal assistance has already been provided in Atlantic Canada to bring new clean coal technologies to the
March 4, 1987_______________COMMONS DEBATES__________________ 3825
point where they can be considered for commercial use. Moreover, in New Brunswick the federal Government provided a $100 million grant and a $350 million loan for the construction of the Point Lepreau nuclear station. That has profound implications for the acid rain effort in the country, because nuclear energy is relatively clean in respect of acid rain.
Other examples of federal Government subventions to the Atlantic provinces for programs and projects in this general area could be cited, including a multi-million dollar electricity subsidy program in my own Province of Prince Edward Island.
I now want to turn to the Canada-U.S. situation. As I mentioned earlier, little progress was made by Canada prior to September, 1984 when the current Government was elected. Some well informed commentators have argued that by the summer of 1984, on the eve of the election of the new Government, the acid rain issue had actually slipped backward to about where it was in 1979 before the Memorandum of Intent was signed by the Governments of Canada and the U.S. Such was the situation that we faced when we took office. With all due respect to the Hon. Member for Davenport, the official spokesman on the environment for the Official Opposition, despite his contentions, we have made progress since September, 1984.
When President Reagan endorsed the report of the Special Envoys, the Prime Minister interpreted his support as a commitment by the U.S. administration to seek from Congress the funds necessary to implement the recommendations. Indeed, the President gave a specific commitment to that effect, I think it was at the news conference when the President endorsed the report.
The President's 1988 budget proposals provided the first opportunity for the United States to honour its commitment to Canada concerning the Special Envoys' report. The initiatives outlined, however, fell substantially short of meeting even the minimum requirements.
The Prime Minister and I gave a clear and unequivocal message to Vice-President Bush at our January 21 meeting in Ottawa. We also made clear to the Vice-President what Canada expects from the United States. I want to conclude on this note. To eliminate acid rain damage and to prevent it from happening in future, Canada is seeking a reduction in the transboundary air pollution flow from the United States to two million metric tonnes of sulphur dioxide per year or about 50 per cent of the 1980 level. We want such a reduction on a targeted and scheduled basis.
As a step toward the objective, we are pressing for full implementation of the Special Envoys' recommendations in a way that achieves early reductions in U.S. emissions affecting Canada. Our objective is based both upon sound scientific information and upon existing principles and obligations under international law that nation states must ensure that activities within their jurisdictions do not damage the environment of other states.

Finally, our objective also extends naturally from the Special Envoys' report itself, which contemplated reductions in "the flow of airborne pollutants across our common border". Our commitment to our objective is strong and unwavering. We will do everything we can to make progress in the time leading up to the next summit between the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada and thereafter. The U.S. administration is having in its words "a fresh look" at its response to the President's commitment in light of the vigorous representations made by the Prime Minister and myself and other Cabinet Ministers to the Vice-President during his visit to Ottawa. Our goal cannot be clearer nor our resolve stronger. We want action, and we want it now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member has asked three questions. I will try to deal with them as expeditiously as I can. On the first question, I am not aware of any lack of support from any colleague within my caucus, let alone from the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett), although obviously we may differ on details, he from the perspective of his province and I from a national perspective.
Second, I do not think the position that I outlined in my remarks today, which echo ones that I have expressed publicly before this occasion, constitute a new position of the Government of Canada. The envoys' report, from memory I think it is on page 4, contemplates a bilateral accord between Canada and the United States, building, more or less in the words of the report, on the spirit of the Memorandum of Intent signed in August, 1980. We have always seen the envoys' process, the report and the recommendations themselves, not as the last step in a long journey but rather as one of the first steps. The scientific evidence is clear. If we are to minimize damage to our ecosystem, to our aquatic life, to our terrestrial features, to our built environment, to our statuary and human health, we have to keep acid rain loadings down to a maximum of 20 kilograms per hectare. If we were to eliminate all sources within Canada of acid rain causing emissions, we still could not achieve that objective because 50 per cent of the emissions affecting Canada cross the border from the United States. In places like the neighborhood of the Hon. Member for Parry

March 4, 1987
Supply
Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) the figure may well be higher. Certainly it is higher in the Haliburton areas in Ontario. We are simply taking the science and translating it into policy. We have to have at least a 50 per cent reduction in U.S. flows into Canada to complement those reductions that we are planning within our own country in order to achieve the maximum acceptable acid rain loadings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two things. I would urge upon the Minister to pay a great deal of attention in the Government's negotiations or discussions with the Americans to the economic approach. Maybe it is a case, as I said before, that the United States of America will not do anything that is not in its self-interest. Because this is probably true, we need to demonstrate just how much it is, not only not in the long term, but in the medium term and even in the short term economic interest of the United States to act with respect to acid rain emissions in its own backyard, both in the Canadian sense and in the American sense of that.
I made the joke earlier about the President at one point thinking that acid rain came from ducks. Just recently we learned, thanks to the Isaac Walton League and a study done by it, that acid rain is actually decimating the population of waterfowl on the East Coast. It is that kind of reality that should be brought home to the Americans.
I have a question for the Minister about the federal-provincial agreements. I must say that I am only now- perhaps I should have seen it earlier-seeing how loose, in a sense, the agreement of 1985 was that was signed at that time.
I have a question about those agreements. Were the amounts of money, which the Minister talked about going to provinces, having to do with acid rain abatement of programs for smelters and what not, for instance, the $20 million for Manitoba, outlined in the agreement of 1985, or are these amounts that have been arrived at subsequently? In other words, what are provinces, which were a party to that agreement in 1985, bound to with respect to actual dollars and cents? What were the expectations or details announced at that time?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLLUTION-EMISSION REDUCTION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member recognizes that I was not the Minister of the Environment at the time the agreement was forged. I can, nevertheless, answer his questions as best I can. There was a general agreement among the federal Government and the seven participating provinces, first, that they would slash their total acid rain emissions by 50 per cent by 1994 based on 1980 figures; second, that each participating province would contribute to
the total effort by slashing its emissions according to a specific schedule agreed upon; third, there was an understanding that the $150 million dollar fund at the federal level to assist the provinces, and through the provinces industry, to achieve the respective provincial control programs, would be used for smelter modernization-pollution abatement, not for thermal power plants, let alone ones operated by the utilities. There were no specific dollar figures attached in February, 1985 on a province by province basis. It was understood, however, that the $150 million would be spent by a rough rule of thumb commensurate with the contribution each province made to the problem. In other words, it was clear, because Quebec and Ontario together accounted for about 80 per cent of the total acid rain-causing emissions in the country, their subvention from the $150 million would be in the neighborhood of 80 per cent of the $150 million fund. In the case of Ontario, because its contribution to the problem was greater than that of Quebec, obviously it would be drawing more heavily from the fund. It was that kind of rough rule of thumb.
When I became Minister, the Minister for the Environment in Ontario almost within days of my appointment came to me and said "We, as a Government, are totally committed to honouring our arrangement within the total deal, but before we can forge a specific control program, especially concerning the four major sources of acid rain pollution within Ontario, we need to have some indication from you, that is from the federal Government, as to our share of the $ 150 million". I, for my part, said, "I cannot very well answer your question until I see your control program and assess what the funding requirement is". It was a chicken and egg kind of thing, a vicious circle, but we agreed on a trade off. Instead of either one of us imposing a requirement on the other, we said, fine, Ontario will rough out its general approach, and for our part we will give Ontario some general idea of how much we think its program would cost and on the basis of an estimated cost what the federal contribution might be toward it from the $150 million. It engaged in that kind of exercise with each of the other provinces. We arrived at the figures I cited, but keep in mind that those are rough figures and in some cases max-imums.
In the case of Ontario, the Government is rightly insisting that the prospective recipient industries demonstrate before the fact that they need a subvention either from the province or from the federal Government because neither of us is in the business of lining the pockets of industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to congratulate my colleague for raising this subject which I believe is of great importance to all Canadians. However, it is of particular importance to residents of the Province of Nova Scotia, a part of which I happen to represent.
While listening to the remarks of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), I was somewhat disappointed that he would not be more specific with regard to what he
March 4, 1987

intends to do to ensure that the provincial Governments abide by the agreements and understandings both in terms of the letter of the law and in terms of its spirit. Perhaps we might spend a few moments on why the federal Minister of the Environment is so reluctant to ask his provincial colleagues in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, to mention just two provinces, to proceed.
Many reasons for this could be offered. I do not think any of them are political, but perhaps they may be. Is it because the present administration in the Province of New Brunswick is due to end its term and that the Minister of the Environment sits by, not so much saying nothing but doing nothing? Is he operating on the instructions of the federal Minister representing New Brunswick in the federal Cabinet to cool it so that the Premier of the province may be able to muscle out a few more votes in the next provincial election?
I think the course that will be followed in New Brunswick is rather evident. That administration will come to an end very soon. Perhaps what is more disturbing is that the federal Minister of the Environment has allowed a very serious situation to become even more serious. He has not taken his responsibilities seriously by trying to enforce the agreements made in those two provinces.
One theory has been advanced by others, but not by me because I would not want to be partisan. It is not my nature. One might say, however, that the people of the Province of Nova Scotia, like our good brothers and sisters in the Province of New Brunswick, are in election mode in a preliminary way. Again, the provincial Minister of the Environment, the Hon. Laird Stirling, is travelling to Ottawa, appearing before the committee and crying great tears of concern. He is telling everyone that he is very concerned, that the Premier is concerned, that the caucus is concerned, that the Conservative executive of his association is concerned, that his mother is concerned and that his sister-in-law is concerned, but he does not take any action.
What does the federal Minister of the Environment do when in Nova Scotia? He just nods his head, continues onward and says nothing. Again, and I say this sincerely, not only does he not say anything but he does not do anything to rectify the serious problem we are now facing as a result of acid rain.
We would have hoped that the Province of Nova Scotia, for example, would have been utilizing funds under the coal technology program. That is not being done. We have heard the great platitudes of the Premier of Nova Scotia who, I might add, has on several occasions changed the entire thrust of the energy policy of Nova Scotia, depending upon where he was speaking. When he is down by the Bay of Fundy, he talks about tidal power. When he is in the Halifax-Dartmouth area, he changes his speech and energy thrust to talk about the offshore oil and gas. When he goes to eastern Nova Scotia, he talks about the utilization of coal from Cape Breton.
We all know that the provincial Crown corporation, the Nova Scotia Power Corporation, utilizes a great deal of coal

produced by the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The emission standards used in the burning of the coal ought to be enforced by the province. We all hope that the Power Corporation will continue to burn that coal, but there are technologies available that are workable and feasible and are in the longterm interests of the people of Nova Scotia, whether they happen to reside in eastern Nova Scotia, Metropolitan Dartmouth-Halifax or indeed Lunenburg, Yarmouth and areas west. The problem is that the Premier of Nova Scotia has abdicated his responsibilities toward the environment and he is being aided and abetted by the federal Minister of the Environment.
In the Legislature which has just recently opened in Nova Scotia, the provincial Leader of the Liberal Party outlined very clearly where he and his Party stood on the issue of acid rain. I think it would do Hon. Members well, and particularly Hon. Members opposite who represent ridings in the Province of Nova Scotia, to examine very clearly what the Leader of the Official Opposition in the Province of Nova Scotia has said. He has said that acid rain poses an immediate and serious threat to the quality of life and economic well-being of the entire Atlantic region. In Nova Scotia, the effects of acid rain are already being severely felt. Eighteen-not one, not two, not three but 18-former salmon streams in the Province of Nova Scotia are no longer able to sustain Fish. That is an appalling number of streams in view of the small size of the Province of Nova Scotia. Another 13 rivers are listed as being endangered. Those rivers are the spawning grounds of the Atlantic salmon and once destroyed, the extinction of the salmon species will not be far behind. Surely as Canadians, whether we reside in Nova Scotia, Ontario, Quebec or the West, we would want to protect and enhance the salmon stocks wherever they may be.
Acid rain which falls in the Maritimes does not originate there but, in my view, in the industrial heartland of the eastern and central regions of North America. The only viable longterm solution to the problem is a major reduction in the industrial emissions which cause acid rain. For this we need international co-operation. Before you seek international cooperation you have to show leadership at home. Leadership is not going to the Canadian Club to amuse different organizations. Leadership is not speaking to different groups across the country. Leadership is taking bold, significant and concrete action which, from time to time, may mean exerting pressure and demanding that the provincial Governments live up to their responsibility as equal partners on this most important issue of acid rain.
The Government is afraid to exercise leadership on this issue both internationally and domestically. Why does the Government refuse to show leadership and demand that the provinces live up to their responsibilities? The conclusion is obvious. The Government does not mean what it said. This is another example of a national Government trying to set national policy with mere platitudes, as it has done, as an analogy, with

March 4, 1987
Supply
regional economic development in eradicating inequalities in this country.
The Government says it is very concerned. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) went to Newfoundland in August of last year and said that our economic development programs are not working. We read that in the Throne Speech, and now we have a new Budget which provides not one new cent or one new innovative program to eradicate the problem of regional economic development. The same is true with regard to the environment and acid rain. The Government has done absolutely nothing to effectuate the positive changes which all Canadians want to see.
Our clean lakes, rivers and streams are one of our greatest natural resources. To sit idly by, as the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is doing, while they are poisoned by industrial contamination would be a criminal act in any jurisdiction in the western world. In Nova Scotia our power plants are almost exclusively generated by coal and oil-fired plants. Our present provincial Government's commitment to reduction of emissions from these plants has been wanting.
For the benefit of members opposite I want to indicate what the official Leader of the Liberal Party in the Province of Nova Scotia said. He said that Nova Scotia has been living up to the letter of agreements concerning reduction of emissions, but has refused to take the lead. He said that a Liberal Government in Nova Scotia would be prepared to show leadership on this issue and serve as an example to other jurisdictions. The technology exists to keep emissions from coal and oil-fired generations to a bare minimum, but that technology costs money. In his opinion the expenditure must be made because the alternative may well be ecologically devastating.
I am glad that my colleague from the New Democratic Party agrees. I am glad once again to see the New Democratic Party following the lead of the Liberal Party in this most important endeavour of trying to control and eradicate the effects of acid rain in this country.
Let us not lose sight of what presently exists. The Government of the Province of Nova Scotia is not doing enough. The federal Government is not helping. It is rewarding the irresponsible behaviour in my Province of Nova Scotia. Economically it is also essential that the acid rain problem be addressed immediately.
Without our inland salmon fishery, the tourist industry in the Provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would suffer a major set-back. Acid rain also poses a distinct threat to various agricultural sectors and to the long-term health of forest related industries.
Due to the federal Minister's failure to exercise his responsibility, we will not only see an exacerbation of the acid rain problem, but direct and consequential effects of the failure to act on behalf of Canadians. Due to his failure to put pressure on the provincial Governments, a very important sector of our economy, namely the tourism sector, will lose great jobproducing potential. The failure of the federal Government to show leadership and make the provincial Governments respond accordingly is telegraphing to all Canadians the message that the Government is not overly concerned about that sector of our economy.
We have heard from numerous sources which have come before different committees of the House of Commons about the effects that acid rain is having on our agricultural sector. In fact, we will hear it again from the Maritime Farmers Council which is meeting tonight. The forest industry is another potential blockbuster employer in the country. If action is not taken immediately by our Governments, that sector, too, will be in great jeopardy.
The Liberal Party, both federally and in the Province of Nova Scotia, advocates immediate remedial action to save our endangered rivers and streams. This can be accomplished through a program of river-bed liming, which has been proven effective in Sweden and in a pilot project on Nova Scotia's south shore. It is not being tried elsewhere in the province as it should be because the province does not want to exercise its responsibility. If that is the case, why does the federal Minister not intervene? The answer is obvious: pending elections. River-bed liming will save the salmon. Admittedly, it is not the long-term solution. However, if we do not save the salmon today, there will not be any left to save in 20 years or more when we finally solve the problem at the source by reducing emissions.
It is very obvious what is taking place. Our tourism, agricultural, forestry and fishery sectors are in danger due to the lack of action by the provincial Government in the Province of Nova Scotia, aided and abetted by the cooperation it is receiving from its federal counterparts in the federal Ministry of the Environment.
The argument about this issue which has been eloquently made by others has not been challenged by the Government, the media or indeed any of the environmentalists. The reason for the lack of action by the provincial Governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and the reason for the irresponsible behaviour by the Minister of the Environment, who is known throughout the Atlantic region as Mr. Clean, is that provincial elections are to take place. If that is not the case, the Premier of New Brunswick and the Premier of Nova Scotia should say so very clearly. However, when this issue is raised, they are never to be found.
It is sad that the provincial Governments have been allowed to abdicate their responsibilities for the serious issue of acid rain and the problems it causes to the sectors of our economy. I hope the Department of the Environment will take concrete steps to ensure that we as Canadians, provincially and federally, exercise our responsibility and live up to our commitments so that we may co-operatively deal with the international situation.
March 4, 1987

The Minister of the Environment must stop acting like a dutiful sheep to the provincial Governments and accept his clear and concrete responsibility as I am sure the former Minister would have done.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on the Hon. Member's speech. Member to turn this into a partisan issue when all of us should be committed to doing whatever we can.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the eloquent comment made by the Hon. Member. She is obviously as concerned as I am about this matter.
Perhaps I can take this opportunity to inform her of the facts. It is a political issue in the Province of Nova Scotia. It is clear that there is an irresponsible Premier there who refuses to exercise the authority that has been given to him by the people of Nova Scotia to try to eradicate acid rain. Furthermore, when it comes to the issue of acid rain in Nova Scotia, the federal Government should be ashamed and embarrassed to set a foot in that province. It has been grossly negligent with regard to that issue.
Let me give two examples. The Minister has told the Board of Trade in Halifax that the provincial Governments must do more. He speaks about emissions from the Nova Scotia Power Corporation as a result of its burning coal. Yet there are two projects before the federal Ministers responsible for regional industrial expansion and the environment that could greatly assist in lessening the emission of acid rain from the burning of coal.
One project is the synfuel project. However, the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion has taken an idiotic partisan attitude toward that synfuel research and development project. With a small amount of money that could be taken from funds already existing in the Governments of Nova Scotia and Canada a pilot project could be initiated dealing with the burning of coal and the lessening of acid rain emissions.
The second example of irresponsibility by the federal Government and the Minister of the Environment concerns the carbogel project that is waiting to be funded by the federal and provincial Governments. Yet the irresponsible Premier of Nova Scotia travels to eastern Nova Scotia to say that his Government has changed its energy policy and will now utilize coal. Everyone in Nova Scotia realizes that the days of
Supply
transporting coal by ship to burn at a power plant are over because of the acid rain problems.
The federal Government must live up to its responsibility and make its provincial counterpart live up to its responsibility to fund the carbogel and synfuel projects jointly because the power generated by the Nova Scotia Power Corporation is derived from coal. Yet the Government, the Minister and the Prime Minister have done nothing other than talk about their concern for acid rain and their concern about coal.
I thank the Hon. Member for her eloquent comment, which gave me an opportunity to explain the irresponsible behaviour and gross negligence of the Minister and the Premier with regard to a very important problem that could be resolved if there was some political will. I can assure the Hon. Member on both counts that they will be gone.

speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for acknowledging the contribution I have made to this debate. The answer to the question is obvious. I do not know of a Government, provincially, federally or municipally, which would say that an acid rain problem could be resolved overnight. I did not even suggest it in debate. What I am suggesting is that there are levers of power in this country, both provincially and federally, which have to be exercised in order to eradicate the problem. Unfortunately, the present administration does not see fit to accept those responsibilities.
In Nova Scotia, with which I am very familiar, we did fund the synfuels project, as one example, so that the emissions from coal would be reduced and reduced substantially. The Tories cut it off. We did fund the carbogel project at the Nova Scotia Power Corporation so that the emissions from coal, again, would be reduced. What have the Tories done? They have cut it off. We did have pilot projects in all the Atlantic regions with regard to the utilization of coal, because it was noted time and time again by the federal Ministry of the Environment that the emissions from coal were a problem. There were pilot projects in New Brunswick in the Colson Cove. There were pilot projects in other parts of Nova Scotia. In fact, even federal and provincial institutions in the Atlantic region did carry out trial projects as well. So there were very

March 4, 1987
Supply
concrete and specific initiatives taken by the previous administration. However, that is not the problem. The problem today is that there is no political will being exercised by the federal Government, nor the provincial Governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, to address this very serious problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLLUTION-EMISSION REDUCTION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me start my contribution to the debate today with some bad news. We have already received the answer from some American representatives to the motion today. The motion reads in part:
That this House also deplores the fact that, two years after the Quebec summit meeting, no benefits to Canada in the form of S02 emission reductions in the United States have materialized; and
That, therefore, this House urges the government to:
(2) request at the April, 1987 summit meeting that the United States reduce
S02 emissions over the Canadian border in a significant manner.
This afternoon CBC Radio at five o'clock ran a story which indicates that the majority leader in the Senate of the United States, Senator Byrd from West Virginia, said that the United States should slow down on its plans for legislation to deal with acid rain. He basically indicated, and I am paraphrasing him, that the case had not been yet proven that S02 emissions were the cause of acid rain and that acid rain, in turn, was causing the problems created both in Canada and in the United States. Lo and behold, he said we have to put more money into research. That is a response from the man whose Party controls the Senate of the United States, and which he leads. He is now parroting the line taken by the President of the United States that more money is needed for research, as opposed to what we believe in this House that more action is needed to do something about the problem.
I would like to focus on a couple of areas during my participation in this debate today. From time to time I have made reference to my previous incarnation as a provincial Member in the Ontario House. Once again I find myself dealing with a topic I dealt with back in 1975-76. That, of course, is the question of the impact of American S02 emissions on Canada and particularly on northwestern Ontario. One of the elements I raised at that time, and I was a voice in the wilderness, was the impact of S02 emissions on the health of human beings.
The District Health Council in my community of Thunder Bay did a study around 1975 and discovered that we had a higher than normal incidence of respiratory disease, not necessarily deaths but diseases of the respiratory system including the lungs. There were those of us who believed at the time that part of the reason for that difference was the apparently high levels of S02 emissions from a couple of our pulp and paper mills and later from an Ontario hydro coal-fired generating station. I did some research in terms of followup and discovered back then, thanks, quite frankly, to the environmental protection agency office out of Duluth, Minnesota, a study conducted in Allegheny County. That is part of the Pittsburgh area. Although I do not have the document handy and I cannot quote the exact figures, the
result of that study was to show the direct relationship between S02 emissions and the health cost in that particular county in the United States. What the study found was that for every 1 per cent reduction in S02 emissions, there was a corresponding savings in terms of American dollars spent on medical aid. The study proved that the benefits of reducing S02 and other airborne contaminants went far beyond the question of saving lakes from acidification and saving our forests, whether it be the maple sugar forests in Quebec or the softwood and hardwood forests in Ontario and elsewhere, from reduced growth. It showed that there was clearly an impact on the health of human beings. I would suggest, and I do not have the specifics to use as verification, that the people who would be affected would be our seniors, our young children and those in other age groups who are more susceptible than others to environmental airborne contaminants.
What we are asking the American Government to do, while clearly of benefit to us here in Canada, is probably of even greater benefit to its own citizens. If by reducing those S02 emissions, the Americans can improve the health of their citizens and reduce the financial burden on their health care system, it is in their best interests. Of course it is in our best interests as well.
I think in a lot of ways Canada as a whole, and I am thinking about the federal as well as the provincial context, has taken those first important steps. We in this country have said to our industries that we have to start cleaning up. We may feel strongly that we have to push them harder, further and faster but, compared to the United States, we have done a fantastic job. Once again in our negotiations, whether by the current federal Government or the previous federal Government, or the provincial Governments, we have not done our job in terms of getting the same deal out of the United States. We have not gone the extra step to not only demand but ensure that promises are actually followed through with dollars and cents. It is clear that the President of the United States has not lived up to his commitment to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney). He has not ensured that Congress has been provided with the amounts of money necessary to pay for the reductions.
The Americans are still listening to the coal lobby. They are still focusing on one part of their country at the expense of another large part of it, and at the expense of the Canadian environment. That has to change. They have to understand that this is not just a Canada-U.S. fight. They must understand that this is a fight between one part of America and another part of America. They have to move quickly, on the one hand, to put in place the necessary reductions and, on the other, to ensure that for those industries directly affected replacement mechanisms are available for those workers who may be displaced. Appropriate assistance must be given to keep these industries intact in order that economies of communities do not suffer. We must do the same in Canada. We can no longer approach the situation in a black and white
March 4, 1987

fashion. We can no longer say that because it is a job we have to keep it regardless of the expense. I think we can have it both ways. We have shown that in Canada, and it is time that the United States agreed to it.
I would like to come back to the health problem. As I mentioned at the beginning of my comments, my interest in the health issue goes back to 1975, which is 12 years ago. A recent report in the United States brought down by the Environmental Protection Agency was covered in an article in The New York Times of February 19, 1987. The report was requested by Lee M. Thomas, Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, in an effort to review its priorities. It was prepared by 75 of the agency's senior professional staff members. I would now like to quote part of the article which states:
The report found that the problems posing the greatest overall risk to human health and the environment in the United States included such conventional air pollutants as sulfur and lead, the destruction of ozone in the atmosphere by manmade chemicals and the risk from pesticides, especially pesticide residues on foods.
Clearly, this report confirms what the Allegheny County study stated back in the 1970s. It also confirms the studies done with respect to the great fogs of London in terms of the impact on the human population. I say to Hon. Members regardless of what Canada and the United States may want to talk about, the United States now has a document which very clearly states that the health of the people of the United States is at risk. Quite clearly it confirms that the health of Canadians is also at risk because of continuing acid rain emissions in this country. They too will have an impact on our health care delivery system.
We hear provincial Governments these days talking about the need to reduce the demand on health care services, and some have imposed user fees. Others try to curtail access. But we could do so much to ease the burden on our health care delivery system in Canada if we would just make a bigger dent in acid rain emissions on both sides of the border. This is clearly an important focus. It is one on which Canadians are in agreement with us.
Results of recent polls indicate that the vast majority of the Canadian public-I believe it is well over two-thirds, if not higher-believe that the environment is the major issue before us today. It is the one about which they are the most concerned. They believe it is important not only to protect our own health, but they want to see our lakes and rivers protected. They do not want to see them killed. They do not want to see fish populations killed off. They do not want to see our forests slowed down in growth. Quite frankly, we cannot afford it. We have not been reforesting as we should have been. In some places there is a danger that we will run out. We are doing research to try to accelerate growth so that the sustainable yield can be improved upon and so that the turn-around time between planting and harvesting can be improved to keep some of our communities viable. The last thing we want to hear is that acid rain is slowing down this growth.
Supply
Acid rain also has an impact on our wildlife in that it gets into the food-chain. Canadians are concerned about this. It is not as if Parliament is going against the grain of the Canadian people by holding back. The people of Canada want us to move forward. They want us to move forward on our own soil. They want us to push the American Government to move forward in the United States. We are of one continent and, yes, we have the longest undefended border in the world. However, acid rain keeps blowing north. The only way we can deal with it is through political pressure from this side of the border and by pressure brought to bear by the people of the United States on their own administration. They must stand up and be counted. They must ensure that their legislators listen to them in the same way that we should be doing here in Canada.
This is an appropriate moment for me to sit down and perhaps respond to any questions that Hon. Members may have.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to what was said by the Hon. Member opposite who spoke to the motion before the House today. His speech focussed mainly on the second part of the motion referring to the failure of the United States to take action on acid rain.
I can assure the Hon. Member that like him, I am very much aware of the health concerns of people living in areas where the effects of acid rain are being felt. I represent the region of Abitibi-Temiscamingue where we have the Noranda mine, and people in their fifties and sixties often have to leave the area because of respiratory diseases. I represent a region that used to be a hunting and fishing paradise, but today, hundreds of lakes are contaminated and our forests are deteriorating. When we realize how important our forests are to the economy of this area, the situation is far from reassuring.
Mr. Speaker, I went into politics for the reasons mentioned by the Hon. Member. I felt that as a citizen, I had certain responsibilities. I wanted things to change, and I felt that the quality of life of my fellow citizens and the quality of our lakes, forests and soils should be one of the responsibilities of our governments. In fact, I welcome this opportunity today to mention that the federal Government has made commitments that will result in $120 million being invested in my riding so that Noranda Mines can install pollution control devices. For future generations, this is a very important step.
My question to the Hon. Member is this: Since his comments dealt with the second part of the motion, would he now have the honesty, as many others have had today, to recognize that, since September 1984, this Government has done more in the fight against acid rain than the previous Liberal Governments, that this Government has set target dates, budgets and S02 emission reduction figures of 50 per cent, and that the provinces will have to do what they are asked? Will he

recognize that the internal measures taken by this Government to fight acid rain are among the most innovative in industrialized countries and certainly much more progressive than what the previous Liberal Government had done?

speechtext:
I wish to thank the Hon. Member for his comments and his question. I am sorry to hear that seniors have been forced to leave his area because of the environment that has been created through industrial development. I know of many people from northwestern Ontario who ended up in Arizona because a doctor told them to go to a place where they can breathe.
There is a situation in one part of my riding called Westport where there is a cold inversion. On extremely cold days when the temperature is minus 30 or 35, a plume from one of the paper mills blankets a residential area. That is the type of thing I am concerned about. I know that the Hon. Member sees the same situation in his own riding.
In response to the Hon. Member's question, I will not use the excuse that I was not here during the previous administration. I was watching it, and some would say that I was a perennial candidate. I would say that there is a difference, and that there has been an improvement. Quite frankly, I have not followed this issue with the same interest as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), although it is one of those issues that I keep my eye on from a distance. I do not believe that enough has been done, although I will admit that there has been some improvement. We must do more, for example like what the Government has done with Noranda in terms of making sure that it can clean up its act. It is one thing to say "thou must", but if the tools are not provided at an acceptable price to the Canadian people, we cannot do our own job within Canada.

speechtext:
I listened with interest to the Hon. Member and his comments relating to the acid rain situation. His comments were illustrated with an oral picture that indicated the problems. All of us share his concerns, and these concerns are common throughout the House and the country. What all of us have a problem with is what can be done that is not presently being done to try to come to grips with this problem?
In his remarks, the Hon. Member said that what had to be done in both the United States and here was the application of political pressure. I am sure that the Hon. Member will agree that there has been a great deal of political pressure exerted on the United States from Canada in one form or another, sometimes by trying to be friendly and negotiate, and sometimes by raising our voice or shaking our fist. I wish to know if the Hon. Member has some other suggestions as to what can be done in the way of political pressure. It is all right to stand in the House and talk about it, use generalities and say that we need more political pressure. But specifically what would the Hon. Member suggest to move us along in this process closer
to the ultimate solution, rather than just talking in terms of generalities, of which all of us are guilty?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLLUTION-EMISSION REDUCTION AGREEMENTS
speechtext: I wish to respond to the Hon. Member's intervention by making two comments. First, the Government must stop pretending that there is progress when there is not. Our position will be undermined with that type of information. More specifically, the Government of Canada could bypass the American administration and go directly to the people of the United States. The Government could pinpoint those crucial areas that are under the acid rain cloud, and talk to the people directly through a media campaign on the radio, in the newspaper, on television, or advertisements, and point out its own studies relating to the health impact, and the impact on the environment of the United States. We could have our embassy staff in Washington arrange to go to those crucial areas and have the American people start lobbying their Representatives and Senators. There is an American election coming up. The primary trail has now started. We should have our people priming Americans who are concerned with the issue to ask those potential presidential candidates where they stand and push them in a direction that will mean better things for both Canada and the United States. We can do that. We have the ability, and it is not against the law. I think we have the responsibility.

Clearly we should start with the premise that the responsibility starts with the owner of a company, whether it is a power company, a steel company, or any company that has emissions. On the other hand, it is people in other areas who are on the receiving end of what comes out of those stacks. Is there not a rationale for the cost of that clean-up being spread? This has been part of the debate in the United States as to who should pay. Should it be only the coal-producing states or the coal-producing areas that pay? Should it be those taxpayers who live within the area that is being hit by acid rain, or should it be the country as a whole? The same debate must occur here. I will give this example. In Ontario we have an opportunity to replace high sulphur American coal with low sulphur western Canadian coal which is mined in British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan. It could be railed through those provinces, plus Manitoba, into Ontario. It could be handled in Thunder Bay, loaded on to a ship, and floated down the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway to hydro plants in southern Ontario.

That would allow Ontario Hydro to reduce its emissions, assuming it decides to go for it. Should it only be the consumers of Ontario Hydro who pay for it, or should the citizens of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec, because they will receive a benefit from it through reduced acid rain emissions, share the load? That is the fundamental question with which the Government must deal in terms of the committee struck by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), along with some of the provinces and some of the industry. speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-POLLUTION-EMISSION REDUCTION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today concerning acid rain and in response to the motion of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). It is an important issue of public interest.
It was interesting to hear a previous speaker mention going directly to the American people on the issue. We have had excellent leadership at the federal level from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), from the Minister, from the Department, and from the Acid Rain Special Committee. The acid rain committee met today with about 14 journalists from the United States. It was an excellent thing to do. The issue is important in our own press, but it seems that it is not sufficiently stated in the American press to stimulate interest and a political will for the American Government to do something. Most of us have friends or relatives living in the United States. In speaking with my sister who lives in Michigan a week or so ago, I told her about our interest, our work, and our commitment to the issue. I also told her how disappointed we were with the administration of the United States. She said: "If you are that concerned, I will phone my Congressman and my Senator". I hope thousands and thousands of American citizens will phone their Congressmen and Senators so that the American Government will keep the commitment it made some two years ago.
The federal Government has established a clear objective for resolving the acid rain problem. Acid deposition must be reduced to less than 20 kilograms per hectare per year in all vulnerable areas. This objective is derived from extensive scientific observation of the effects of acid rain in Canada and is supported by scientific information from other countries.
To achieve the objective, total Canadian sulphur dioxide emissions from the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border eastward must be reduced to 2.3 million tonnes per year or 50 per cent of the 1980 level. Also, the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide from the United States into eastern Canada must be reduced to about two million tonnes or about 50 per cent of the 1980 level.
The Canadian acid rain abatement program is well under way. Quebec and Ontario have already introduced regulatory programs. Quebec will achieve emission reductions of 45 per cent by 1990. Ontario will achieve its emission reduction of 60

per cent, or 10 per cent more than it was originally committed to, by 1994. Manitoba recently issued draft regulations to achieve its 25 per cent reduction in emissions by 1994.
Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island have air pollution control initiatives which will achieve the 25 per cent and 16 per cent reductions required respectively by 1994. Regulatory and program measures to achieve more than 90 per cent of the emission reductions under the Canadian acid rain abatement program are now in place.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is now in the process of negotiating formal federal-provincial acid rain abatement agreements to ratify and make binding this part among Governments. There can be no backsliding from the commitments which have been made. All eight Governments must show their clear determination to deliver.
The federal Government has done so. Let me cite a few examples. Through the Industrial and Regional Development Program of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the federal Government has assisted Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting in Manitoba to demonstrate commercially a new process which would reduce emissions from the plant by about 35 per cent. Under the same program, Inco and Falconbridge in Ontario are being assisted in the commercial demonstration of technologies in time for the December 1988 decisions called for in Ontario's regulations. To date, only Noranda has submitted a request for financial assistance for smelter modernization-pollution abatement. A cost sharing agreement with Quebec and Noranda is expected to be concluded shortly.
Substantial progress has also been made under the coal utilization demonstration program of Energy, Mines and Resources. Alternative coal combustion systems, including fluid bed combustion, coal-water mixtures, coal preparation and improved burner systems, have advanced to the point where they can be considered for commercial use.
The federal Government's research and monitoring program has also produced some significant findings. Studies in Nova Scotia have shown that the emission reductions, which have taken place over the past 15 years or so, have cut the acid deposition in some areas to less than 20 kilograms per hectare per year-the level required under the abatement program. The rivers in those areas are starting to show signs of chemical recovery. Not only is this good news, but it clearly demonstrates Canada is on the right track with its abatement program and objectives.
Since the western coal task force released its report in August 1986, there has been considerable discussion in a variety of forums on the subject of using more western Canadian coal to reduce Ontario Hydro's acid gas emissions.
Environment Canada recognizes that low sulphur western coal has the potential to reduce emissions substantially. Because there would be considerable benefits to the country, we are encouraged to see that Ontario Hydro is committed to full consideration of the role western coal could play in its emission reduction plans.

March 4, 1987
Supply
We are encouraged that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) met just this week with Premier Peterson. They have agreed to establish a committee involving themselves and the western Premiers. The purpose will be to explore opportunities for improving the economic competitiveness of western coal in Ontario. I applaud the initiative of the Deputy Prime Minister in this particular regard.
Not only will the Canadian acid rain abatement program reduce the damage Canada is doing to itself, it will also reduce the transboundary flow of air pollution from Canada into the eastern United States. In 1980 the transboundary flow from Canada to the United States was about 1.5 million tonnes. By 1994 this will be reduced to about 0.8 million tonnes. This should help alleviate some of the damage being caused in the northeastern United States. In the Adirondacks, for instance, as much as 25 per cent of the acid rain which falls is of Canadian origin. By significantly reducing our contribution to acid rain damage in these areas, Canada is honouring its international obligation not to pollute other countries to the extent of injury to human health or property.
More than half of the acid deposition in eastern Canada comes from U.S. emissions. Areas such as Muskoka-Halibur-ton through to Quebec City receive about three-quarters of their acid deposition from the United States. In 1980, about four million tonnes of sulphur dioxide flowed across the border into eastern Canada. In order that acid rain damage be eliminated, Canada is seeking a reduction in the transboundary air pollution flow to about 2 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide per year and implementation of a U.S. program to reduce the transboundary flows to this level on a targeted and scheduled basis.
What the United States does to honour its commitment and how it does it are its own legitimate domestic decisions. Whether the transboundary flows are reduced to the level required is Canada's business. With this in mind, we should judge the extent of our satisfaction with U.S. actions not by dollars spent or technology used, however important that is,
but rather by what really matters, reductions in transboundary flows of air pollution.
Canada and the United States have a long and outstanding history of resolving transboundary environmental problems. The special envoys on acid raid put what needed to be done rather well in their report, and I quote:
The foundations of that response-the joint statement and the memorandum of intent-are already in place. A precedent for that response already exists in the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement.
What remains is to borrow from that precedent and build upon those foundations a bilateral accord which will jointly address a common problem in the best tradition of U.S.-Canadian environmental relations. We know exactly what should be in that accord and we are prepared to meet our obligations to the United States. We want the Americans to do likewise.
